title: Ionic Memory and Computing
intro: Synthetic ionic materials could offer a route to brain-like computing. Realizing that potential requires understanding how their chemistry enables them to process, retain, and transmit information.
caption: Biological signaling, artificial neural networks, and ionic devices that reproduce aspects of neuronal function.
background_html: The growing computational demands of AI make energy-efficient information processing increasingly important. The brain offers a different model: it learns and remembers through regulated ion flow, rather than the electronic currents used in conventional computers.

title: Selective Ion Transport
intro: In synthetic pores, however, selective binding does not necessarily lead to selective passage. Understanding how pore chemistry governs ion entry, binding, and release could guide more efficient separations with less waste.
caption: Ion-channel-inspired membrane concepts for separating rare-earth ions.
background_html: Rare-earth elements are essential to magnets used in electric vehicles and wind turbines, but their chemical similarity makes separation difficult and resource-intensive. Biological molecules show how subtle differences between ions can produce strong selectivity.

title: Interfacial Molecular Recognition
intro: Understanding how surfaces shape molecular recognition could make receptor design more predictive, extend continuous monitoring to new targets, and broaden access to diagnostics beyond the laboratory.
caption: Target recognition by biological receptors and by receptors attached to sensing electrodes.
background_html: Continuous glucose monitors show what real-time molecular sensing can offer, yet most other molecules still require laboratory testing. A central obstacle is finding receptors that recognize their targets reliably when attached to an electrode.

title: Researcher-Directed Automation
background_html: Molecular simulation can help explain experimental measurements and identify promising directions for discovery. Its wider use, however, is limited by the time researchers spend preparing and running calculations and processing results. Reducing this repetitive work could make computational insight available to more experimental studies and leave more time for developing questions and interpreting the underlying science.
intro: This research explores how AI-assisted automation can support molecular simulation while keeping scientific judgment with the researcher. The broader goal is to make computation a more practical partner in experimental discovery: helping researchers examine more hypotheses, reduce trial and error, and use experimental time and resources more effectively.
caption: Computation-guided experimental discovery. Candidates and screening outcomes are illustrative, not reported results. The robotic arms represent software-based automation, not physical laboratory robots.
alt: Conceptual illustration linking researcher direction, computational automation, illustrative candidate screening, and experimental studies.
